strengths: Identifies a well-motivated and practically important limitation of spectral IV methods (SpecIV): learned features are outcome-agnostic and can fail when the structural function is poorly aligned with the top singular subspace of the conditional expectation operator T. This diagnosis is grounded in and builds constructively on very recent theory (Meunier et al. 2025).

The proposed fix is elegant and principled: augmenting T with a rank-one (or higher-rank) term aligned with r0=E[Y|Z], and showing (Proposition 1) that the resulting contrastive loss exactly targets the best low-rank approximation of the augmented operator. The derivation via the equivalent joint loss over (theta, omega) to avoid differentiating through matrix inverses is a sensible practical touch.

Nontrivial theoretical contributions: a new high-probability (rather than in-expectation) generalization bound for the 2SLS estimator under sub-Gaussian noise (Theorem 1), and a careful perturbation-theoretic analysis (Wedin sin-Theta based) relating the singular subspaces of the augmented operator back to those of T, yielding explicit 'good' and 'bad' scenario corollaries that quantify when a single learned feature suffices instead of k features under standard SpecIV.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: a fully controlled synthetic study isolating the effect of misalignment (c_alpha) and singular-value decay (c_sigma), a new harder dSprites benchmark (h_new, based on ellipse orientation) constructed with an explicit argument for why it is a genuinely 'bad' case (backed by empirical spectral alignment diagnostics in Appendix D.2), and an OPE application demonstrating broader applicability beyond the core causal estimation setting.

Honest and useful discussion of limitations, notably Appendix D.8's frank admission that hyperparameter selection for delta via minimizing the 2SLS/stage-2 loss lacks theoretical justification, and the paper explicitly flags that the higher-rank extension (Section E) is preliminary and left for future theoretical work.
weaknesses: The main generalization bound (Theorem 4 and its 'good'/'bad' corollaries) depends critically on the optimality gap E_d(theta, omega, delta), which quantifies how well the neural-network-trained features approximate the population truncated SVD of the augmented operator. The paper explicitly states that bounding this quantity is an 'open problem,' meaning the headline theoretical guarantees are conditional on an unquantified term, leaving the overall statistical guarantee incomplete in practice.

Selection of the key hyperparameter delta remains largely heuristic. The paper offers two imperfect strategies (loss-balancing heuristic and an alignment-projection estimator) but acknowledges neither has firm theoretical backing, and results (e.g., Figure 2, cases where increasing delta beyond a certain point degrades performance) show sensitivity to this choice, which could hinder reproducibility and practical adoption.

The OPE experiments (Section 6.3) do not show a uniformly compelling advantage: no method dominates across environments, and AugSpecIV and DFIV show opposite strengths/weaknesses on Cartpole vs. Mountain Car, weakening the claim that the method 'remains robust and competitive' in this setting.

The higher-rank perturbation extension, which is conceptually important for more general outcome-aware augmentation (e.g., multiple moments of Y), is only sketched with limited theory and a small, inconclusive K=2 experiment (Figure 14), so the paper's applicability beyond the rank-one case is not yet well established.

The work is closely derivative of a very recent, seemingly concurrent companion paper (Meunier et al. 2025, cited throughout as the source of the 'good/bad' framework and much of the notation/technical machinery), which somewhat limits the independent originality of the theoretical framing, even though the outcome-aware augmentation itself is a genuine and useful extension.

The paper is notation-heavy and dense (extensive operator-theoretic machinery, many assumptions with implicit interdependencies such as positivity of ill-posedness measures and spectral gaps), which may limit accessibility and make it harder for practitioners to verify when the theoretical conditions actually hold for their data.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated failure mode of SpecIV (outcome-agnostic feature learning failing under spectral misalignment) and proposes a principled fix via an augmented operator T_delta with an accompanying contrastive loss (Proposition 1) that has a clean operator-theoretic interpretation.

The theoretical analysis is fairly comprehensive: a non-asymptotic, high-probability 2SLS generalization bound (Theorem 1) that improves on prior in-expectation results, and a perturbation-theoretic analysis (Theorem 4, using Wedin's sin-Theta theorem) that characterizes how the augmented operator's dominant subspaces relate to those of the original T in both 'good' and 'bad' alignment regimes.

The paper contributes a new, harder dSprites benchmark (h_new based on ellipse orientation) with supporting empirical justification (Section D.1-D.2) that the standard benchmark is spectrally well-aligned and hence not diagnostic of the claimed failure mode.

Experiments span three settings (synthetic, semi-synthetic dSprites, and off-policy evaluation in RL), showing the method broadens applicability of spectral IV methods to non-compact-operator settings via an iterative scheme.

Practical guidance for selecting the hyperparameter delta is provided along with a diagnostic (Proposition 2) for estimating alignment of h0 with learned features, which is a useful applied contribution.
weaknesses: The core theoretical vehicle (the 'good'/'bad' scenario characterization, T-based perturbation theory) is inherited almost directly from a very recent, closely related paper (Meunier et al. 2025, arXiv:2506.10899); the present work's novelty largely consists of a fairly simple rank-one augmentation of the loss/operator, making the conceptual leap relatively incremental despite the technical depth of the appendix.

The generalization bound in Theorem 4/16 depends on the optimality gap E_d(theta,omega,delta), which the paper explicitly states cannot be bounded without architecture-specific DNN generalization results for the spectral contrastive loss ('an open problem in its own right'). This leaves the headline theoretical guarantee incomplete/non-actionable in terms of sample complexity or network design.

Selection of the key hyperparameter delta is entirely heuristic: the paper offers two ad hoc strategies (loss-balancing heuristic and stage-2 loss minimization) and explicitly admits in Section D.8 that minimizing the second-stage 2SLS loss for model/delta selection lacks theoretical justification and that there is 'no clear way' to justify it rigorously. This undermines the practical usability of the method, since good performance is 'contingent on the choice of δ.'

The extension to higher-rank augmentations (multiple outcome moments), which would be needed for more realistic multi-dimensional outcome information, is left essentially unanalyzed theoretically, and the reported preliminary experiments (Section E, Figure 14) are inconclusive ('differences are small and do not allow strong conclusions').

Empirical gains are mixed and sometimes modest: on the well-aligned dSprites task the improvement is only ~20%; on the harder task the method merely matches or slightly exceeds DFIV rather than clearly surpassing it; and in the OPE experiments no method (including AugSpecIV) performs uniformly well across environments, with DFIV comparisons undermined by the authors' own admission of hyperparameter-sampling-induced baseline weakness.

Experimental rigor is limited: only 9 independently fitted models per configuration for the main dSprites comparison, no formal significance testing, and the synthetic experiments' benefit of δ appears sensitive to the decay/alignment regime (e.g., in Figure 2, cα=1.0 with cσ=0.8 shows little to no improvement at small δ), suggesting the practical benefit is narrower than the framing in the abstract/introduction suggests.

The construction of h_new (using ad hoc image heuristics like max-pooling over rows/columns after Gaussian smoothing to isolate orientation) feels engineered specifically to produce a misaligned function for T, raising some concern about how representative this constructed benchmark is of real misalignment scenarios encountered in practice.

strengths: Clear identification of a real limitation of prior spectral IV methods (SpecIV/Meunier et al.): outcome-agnostic feature learning fails under spectral misalignment. The motivation is well-grounded in recent theory (Meunier et al. 2025) and the paper builds directly and coherently on this gap.

The proposed augmented operator T_delta and the associated contrastive loss (Eq. 4/5) are elegant and simple: a rank-one augmentation of the operator with r0 that can be optimized without backpropagating through matrix inverses via the auxiliary variable trick. Proposition 1 cleanly establishes the equivalence between minimizing the loss and finding the best low-rank approximation of T_delta.

Strong theoretical contribution: a new non-asymptotic, high-probability generalization bound for the 2SLS estimator (Theorem 1) that improves on prior in-expectation results (e.g., Chen & Christensen), combined with a careful perturbation analysis (Wedin sin-theta based) that explicitly connects the singular subspaces of the augmented operator back to those of the original operator T, yielding explicit bounds in both the 'good' and 'bad' alignment regimes (Theorem 4 and its corollaries).

The paper explicitly quantifies the benefit of the method in the 'bad' scenario: showing that one feature (d=1) with a well-chosen delta can recover a structural function aligned with an arbitrarily deep singular direction v_k, whereas standard SpecIV would require learning k features. This is a crisp, interpretable theoretical payoff.

Thorough and diverse experimental validation: controlled synthetic experiments with tunable spectral alignment (c_alpha, c_sigma), a new and more challenging dSprites benchmark (h_new based on ellipse orientation) motivated and justified via spectral alignment diagnostics (Section D.1-D.2), and an off-policy evaluation application showing the method's applicability beyond the core causal-inference setting.

Good practical treatment of the delta-selection problem: the paper offers multiple practical heuristics (loss-balancing, alignment estimation via Proposition 2, stage-2 loss), is honest about their lack of full theoretical justification (Section D.8 candidly discusses why stage-2 loss minimization lacks decomposition guarantees), and empirically cross-validates that these heuristics agree in practice (Figure 13).
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4 and its corollaries) depend on the optimality gap E_d(theta_hat_m, omega_hat_m, delta), which the paper explicitly states requires 'architecture-specific generalization bounds for DNN training with the spectral contrastive loss, an open problem in its own right.' This leaves a significant gap between the population-level analysis and what is actually achievable by a trained neural network, somewhat limiting the practical bite of the end-to-end guarantees.

The paper's own experiments show that performance is quite sensitive to delta, and larger delta can degrade performance substantially (e.g., delta=3.0 or 1.0 in Figure 3 right / Figure 4), while no theoretically justified selection procedure for delta is provided; the recommended heuristic (balancing loss terms) is admittedly ad hoc and the alternative (stage-2 loss minimization) is explicitly acknowledged to lack theoretical grounding (Section D.8).

The higher-rank extension (multiple outcome functions, Section E) is only sketched with preliminary, inconclusive experiments ('differences are small and do not allow strong conclusions at this stage'), and full theoretical analysis for K>1 is deferred to future work, so the paper's applicability to more complex, higher-dimensional outcome-relevant signals is not yet established.

In the OPE experiments, results are mixed: no method (including AugSpecIV) uniformly outperforms baselines across the three environments (Cartpole/MountainCar/Catch), and delta is tuned per-environment as a hyperparameter via search rather than through a principled adaptive procedure, which weakens the practical/generalizable value of the OPE results as evidence of robustness.

The comparison set of baselines, while reasonable (DFIV, KIV, SpecIV), does not include some more recent minimax/adversarial NPIV approaches or other kernel-based adaptive feature methods mentioned in the related work section, so the empirical superiority claim is somewhat narrower than the literature review might suggest.

The rank-one perturbation is restricted to using r0=E[Y|Z] (or a single moment); the choice of which outcome-derived quantity to use for the augmentation is itself somewhat ad hoc and its optimality relative to alternative augmentations is not theoretically characterized.

strengths: Identifies a well-motivated and clearly articulated limitation of existing spectral-feature NPIV methods (outcome-agnostic feature learning failing under spectral misalignment), building naturally on recent work (Sun et al. 2025; Meunier et al. 2026).

The augmented operator Tδ and the associated contrastive loss are elegantly derived, with a clean equivalence (Proposition 4.1) between minimizing the new loss and finding a low-rank approximation of the augmented operator, avoiding unstable backprop through matrix inverses via a joint (θ, ω) parameterization.

Comprehensive theoretical treatment: a new high-probability (rather than in-expectation) 2SLS error bound under sub-Gaussian noise, an explicit loss-to-operator-gap bound (Proposition A.4) that is stated to be novel even for the δ=0 (SpecIV) case, and explicit characterization of both 'good' and 'bad' alignment regimes showing dimensionality benefits of the proposed method.

Strong empirical validation across three complementary settings: fully controlled synthetic data, a new and more challenging dSprites benchmark (ellipse orientation) explicitly designed to break spectral alignment, and an off-policy evaluation application, showing consistent benefits of δ>0 in misaligned regimes.

Unusually thorough appendix work: multiple practical strategies for selecting δ, an honest discussion of the lack of theoretical justification for the common practice of tuning via 2SLS validation loss, comparison against naive two-stage outcome-aware baselines showing why the proposed joint objective is needed, and a preliminary extension to higher-rank (multi-functional) augmentations.

Honest, well-reasoned limitations discussion (e.g., admitting that proving DNN training drives the excess loss to zero is left open, and that stage-2 loss minimization for model selection lacks theoretical backing).
weaknesses: Selection of the key hyperparameter δ remains heuristic in practice; none of the three proposed strategies (alignment estimation, loss-balancing, stage-2 loss minimization) has a rigorous justification, and the paper itself concedes this is an open methodological gap, which somewhat undercuts the practical usability of the method.

The downstream 2SLS guarantees are conditional on the representation-learning optimality gap Ed(θ,ω,δ) being small; the paper explicitly does not prove that empirical DNN training drives the augmented contrastive loss to its population optimum, leaving a significant gap between the theory and what is actually verified in practice.

The contribution, while technically substantial, is an incremental (rank-one) extension of a very recent existing framework (SpecIV / Meunier et al. 2026); the core novelty is the outcome-aware augmentation rather than a fundamentally new estimation paradigm, and the higher-rank generalization needed for genuinely multivariate/vector-valued outcomes is only sketched with limited empirical support and no theory.

OPE experiments show mixed, non-uniform results (no method dominates across CartPole/Catch/Mountain Car), weakening the claimed practical robustness story in that application and making it harder to assess real gains from the outcome-aware modification in this setting.

All empirical validation is synthetic or semi-synthetic (dSprites, OPE simulators); no real-world econometric IV application (e.g., along the lines of the schooling/wage motivating example) is used to demonstrate practical impact.

The reproducibility link for code is left as a placeholder in the manuscript, and some experimental design choices (e.g., manually reduced feature dimensionality relative to prior work, post-hoc rejection rules for unstable baseline predictions) are somewhat ad hoc and could affect the fairness of comparisons to DFIV/KIV.

strengths: Identifies a well-motivated and concrete limitation of existing spectral IV methods (SpecIV): outcome-agnostic feature learning fails under spectral misalignment between h0 and the top singular functions of T. The paper builds directly and coherently on this diagnosis (from Meunier et al. 2026) rather than merely restating it.

The core methodological idea—augmenting the conditional expectation operator T with an extra 'column' aligned with r0 and showing (Proposition 4.1) that minimizing the proposed contrastive loss is equivalent to learning the truncated SVD of this augmented operator—is elegant, simple to implement (via an auxiliary linear head ω), and naturally reduces to standard SpecIV when δ=0.

Comprehensive and rigorous theoretical analysis: a new high-probability (rather than in-expectation) generalization bound for the 2SLS estimator under sub-Gaussian noise (Theorem 5.1), a general excess-loss-to-operator-gap bound (Proposition A.4) that is stated to be novel even for the δ=0 case, and detailed perturbation-theoretic analysis (Wedin sin-Θ based) explicitly characterizing the 'good' and 'bad' alignment regimes and how augmentation provably helps recover h0 with far fewer features in the bad regime.

Experimental validation is reasonably thorough: fully controlled synthetic experiments isolating the effect of alignment and singular-value decay, a thoughtfully constructed and justified new dSprites benchmark specifically designed to stress spectral misalignment (with supporting analysis in Appendix E.1–E.2 showing the original benchmark is 'easy' and the new one is 'hard'), and an off-policy evaluation application demonstrating broader applicability of the operator-learning perspective.

The paper is unusually transparent about the limits of its own heuristics: it explicitly acknowledges that a common practical model-selection method (minimizing 2SLS loss) lacks theoretical justification (Section E.8), discusses numerical instabilities in the alignment-based δ-selection heuristic, and compares against 'naive' outcome-aware baselines to demonstrate that the specific construction is not trivial (Appendix G).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees and the operator characterization are developed only for rank-one augmentation; the higher-rank (multi-outcome-moment) extension is only sketched with a single, inconclusive preliminary experiment (Figure 16), leaving open how the framework scales to richer outcome information.

Selection of the key hyperparameter δ remains fundamentally heuristic in practice: three different strategies are proposed (alignment estimation, loss-balancing, 2SLS cross-validation) but none has full theoretical backing, and the alignment-based estimator is noted to become numerically unstable as δ grows, which somewhat undercuts the practical usability of the method despite its theoretical appeal.

Guarantees in Section 5 are conditional on the empirical DNN feature learning achieving small population excess loss Δδ; the paper explicitly leaves open whether/how gradient-based training of the contrastive objective actually attains this, so the end-to-end statistical theory is incomplete for the deep-learning implementation actually used in experiments.

The empirical validation, while including a genuinely more challenging dSprites variant, still relies substantially on benchmarks constructed by the authors themselves to expose the failure mode being fixed, and the OPE experiments show no method (including the proposed one) dominating uniformly across tasks, somewhat softening the practical significance claims.

The manuscript is dense and notation-heavy (operator/functional analysis throughout the main text), which may limit accessibility despite the topic's practical relevance to causal inference practitioners.
